title: Tiny Snakes Roll to Escape Danger, Four Times Faster Than Slithering
summary:
Imagine a tiny snake that does not slither away from danger. It rolls! Dwarf reedsnakes in Southeast Asia can roll about four times faster than they slither, and scientists have worked out how they do it.

Rolling sounds easy, but for an animal it is hard. A wheel turns around a fixed axle while the load it carries stays still. An animal has no axle, so if its whole body spins, its head spins too, making balance and steering much harder.

Scientists filmed the snakes from several angles. While rolling, they reached peak speeds of 1.72 to 3.69 metres per second, about four times their fastest slithering speed. Even at that speed, they stayed on a racetrack only 20 centimetres wide, so this is not wild tumbling.

Their secret is careful timing. They roll on one side, then swing a curved part of the body downward beside the head, a move researchers called a stroke. With each cycle, the side touching the ground switches. Best of all, the head stays out of the spin and points forward, like a steady lookout.
why_it_matters: It shows how animals can solve a tricky movement problem in a clever way, just like you might find a faster way to do something hard.

keywords.explanation: To slither is to slide along the ground the way a snake does.
An axle is the bar in the middle of a wheel that the wheel turns around.
Here, a stroke is one special swing of the snake's body that helps it roll.
Dwarf reedsnakes are a kind of very small snake that lives in Southeast Asia.
Tumbling means rolling over and over without control.

background_read: Snakes usually move by slithering, sliding their bodies along the ground.
Rolling is a much faster way to escape, but it is hard for an animal because it has no wheel or axle to spin around.
Scientists filmed these tiny snakes to learn how they roll without losing their balance.
